title: Pediatric GI, Part 2: Upper and lower GI

sections.title: Esophageal atresia and rumination
notes: Esophageal atresia: choking with feeds, **NG tube will not pass**.
Rumination: effortless regurgitation of recent food, often with psychosocial stress. **Multidisciplinary and behavioural therapy**.

sections.title: Reflux (GER vs GERD)
notes: Happy spitter: peaks around 4 months, **gone by 12 to 24 months**, reassure.
Trial **thickened feeds or a 2-week hydrolyzed formula** (or maternal dairy elimination if breastfed) to test for cow's milk protein allergy.
Severe GERD failing treatment: GI referral, **fundoplication** last resort.

sections.title: Eosinophilic esophagitis
notes: Eosinophils infiltrate the esophagus, driven by **food allergy**.
Vomiting, chest or epigastric pain, dysphagia, **food impaction** in a teen. Suspect when acid suppression fails.
Diagnosis: **endoscopy with biopsy**. Treat with diet elimination, PPI or swallowed steroids, repeat scopes.

sections.title: Pill esophagitis
notes: History is key: pill (doxycycline, NSAIDs, iron) taken with little water before lying down.
Treat by stopping the pill, drink a full glass of water upright.

sections.title: Foreign body ingestion
notes: Most common at **6 months to 3 years**. Get x-rays, but food, wood, plastic and aluminum can be invisible.
Coin vs **button battery**: battery has a halo (double ring).
**Battery in the esophagus: remove immediately**. Symptomatic: remove. Blunt asymptomatic coin in the esophagus: can wait up to 24 hours.

sections.title: Caustic ingestion
notes: **Alkali** may show no mouth burns but deep esophageal injury. Acids injure the stomach. A clean mouth does not rule out injury.
Drooling, dysphagia, abdominal pain, stridor.
**Do not neutralize or induce vomiting**. Endoscopy 12 to 24 hours after (not after about 5 days). Late complication: **strictures**.

sections.title: Vomiting differential: UTI and appendicitis
notes: Always **test the urine** in a vomiting child.
Appendicitis in young children can present with vomiting with or without pain or fever.

sections.title: Cyclic vomiting syndrome
notes: Stereotyped episodes of intense vomiting with **normal health between**. Associated with **family history of migraine** (migraine equivalent).
Treat with hydration, antiemetics, migraine prophylaxis.

sections.title: Upper GI bleeding
notes: Endoscopy shows the bleeding site. Causes: Mallory-Weiss tear, ulcers, varices.

sections.title: Pyloric stenosis
notes: **3 to 6 weeks**, first-born boys. **Nonbilious projectile vomiting**, hungry after vomiting, olive mass.
**Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis**. Correct fluids and electrolytes before surgery.
Ultrasound: **muscle thickness over 4 mm, length over 14 mm**. Treat with pyloromyotomy.

sections.title: Duodenal atresia and annular pancreas
notes: Bilious vomiting on day 1, **polyhydramnios**, **double bubble**. Rare (1 in 10,000). **Down syndrome in 20 to 30%**.
Look for other anomalies (heart, spine). Correct electrolytes, NG decompression, **surgical repair**.
Annular pancreas: also obstructs the duodenum, also linked to Down syndrome.

sections.title: Functional constipation
notes: Triggers: toilet training, stress, travel, holding stool. Large hard stools, painful.
Pain can be dramatic and mimic an acute abdomen. Ask about stooling history.
**Encopresis** is overflow soiling, not diarrhea.

sections.title: Constipation treatment
notes: Impaction: **clean out first** (enema or PEG through NG), then maintenance.
Maintenance: **polyethylene glycol daily**, safe long term, plus behaviour (sit 10 minutes after meals) and more water and fibre.

sections.title: Hirschsprung disease
notes: Associated with **Down syndrome**. **No meconium in 48 hours** (99% of healthy term babies pass it).
Aganglionic segment is narrow, proximal bowel dilated. Explosive stool after rectal exam.
Complication: **enterocolitis**. Diagnosis: rectal suction biopsy. Treat with resection and pull-through.

sections.title: Anal fissure
notes: Bright red blood on hard stool, painful passage. Treat the constipation, sitz baths.

sections.title: Recurrent abdominal pain and IBS
notes: One of the most common reasons to see a pediatrician, about 15 to 35% of children.
**Red flags**: weight loss, night waking pain, GI bleeding, fever, family history of IBD, pain away from the umbilicus.
IBS: cramping pain relieved by stooling, with change in stool frequency or form.

sections.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
notes: Bloody diarrhea, weight loss, growth delay, arthritis. **Ulcerative colitis**: continuous from the rectum. Crohn: skip lesions, perianal disease, ileum.
**Pyoderma gangrenosum** (looks like a spider bite, then ulcer) and erythema nodosum. Toxic megacolon: plain x-ray first.
Rule out infection with stool cultures before diagnosing IBD. Diagnosis by colonoscopy with biopsy.

sections.title: Celiac disease
notes: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes on biopsy.
Treatment: lifelong **gluten-free diet** (no barley, rye, wheat).

sections.title: Cystic fibrosis (GI)
notes: CFTR chloride transport defect. **Pancreatic insufficiency in about 90%**.
Failure to thrive in the first months with **bulky greasy foul stools**: test for CF.
72-hour fecal fat is the accurate test for fat malabsorption. Sweat chloride for diagnosis. Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
